by expounding the True Dharma, the Jewel of the Dharma is made inexhaustible; and...
By upholding the practice of the precepts, the Jewel of the Sangha remains unbroken;
this applies equally to oneself and others.
Sūtra: Subduing the enmity of Māra and restraining all non-Buddhists.
The commentary states:
This reveals the merit of being able to crush enemies.
"Māras" refers to the four māras, or alternatively, the eight māras.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that by adding four inversions to the previous four, one who harbors these eight qualities is called a Māra.
A Māra is an enemy, for he is an enemy of the Dharma.
The subduing of all māras is explained in a separate chapter.

As for the four inversions (catur-viparyāsa), which are the conceptual grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha), they are permanently severed upon the first bhūmi and gradually suppressed prior to the bhūmis.
"Restraint" means to control, as in restraining oxen or horses.
By possessing wisdom and eloquence, one can subdue the non-Buddhists;
by drawing near to the Ten Powers, one can subdue the devas and Māras.
Approaching the four fearlessnesses, one is able to subdue the heterodox teachers.
The Sūtra says: "Forever free from all obstacles, hindrances, and entanglements.
The commentary states:
This reveals the bodhisattva’s merit of being free from defilement.
"Obstruction" refers to that which hinders; there are two kinds:
first, the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has as its essence the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions and secondary afflictions abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms.

The cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) has as its essential nature all factors abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms that obstruct wisdom, such as attachment, ignorance, pride, and so forth.
Regarding the number [of bodhisattvas], whether the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are suppressed or abandoned gradually or all at once, it is all as explained in the treatise.

At this stage of the eighth ground (*bhūmi*), all active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two hindrances within the six consciousnesses have been entirely suppressed, or their seeds have already been severed; therefore, it is said that they "seek liberation."
"Covering" (*nīvaraṇa*) refers to that which obscures the mind of the practitioner, preventing it from becoming pure.
There are five such types: first, the hindrance of sensual desire;
second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and regret; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt.
These five constitute obstacles during three periods.

Desire for the five sensory objects can obstruct one from leaving the household life; once one has left the household life, having previously committed sexual misconduct, there is the awakening [to this fault].
Hostility acts as an obstacle; failing to awaken, one gives rise to further hostility.
If one does not commit unwholesome conduct, yet encounters obstacles when training in concentration and wisdom:
first, when beginning to settle the mind, drowsiness and lethargy act as obstacles.
Next, one trains in uplifting the mind, for restlessness and remorse act as obstacles;
if one abides in the state of equanimity, doubt can act as an obstacle.
These five hinder the antidotes.
Therefore, they are established as *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances).
As for the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), they are called "envelopments" because they repeatedly arise and envelop the mind of the practitioner; thus, they are established as *paryavasthānas*.

These are of eight kinds: namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
The first two [hindrances] obstruct morality; the next two obstruct meditative concentration; the following two obstruct wisdom;

and the final two types obstruct the welfare of oneself and others, because for those who have left the household life, these frequently manifest through the gateway of stinginess and envy regarding their own and others' welfare.
The two obstacles already encompass all defilements; among them, the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are specifically cited because they are predominant.
The three outflows (*āsrava*), the four graspings (*upādāna*), the bodily fetters (*kāyabandhana*), and the bonds (*bandhana*) are all understood to be abandoned accordingly.

The older translation says, "All are already purified," which is difficult to understand in terms of its textual meaning; it refers to the exhaustion of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). The Sūtra states:
"Through mindfulness and concentration, when the time for total [attainment] arrives, one reaches the gateway of the wisdom of liberation."
The commentary states:
The first two lines describe the merit of being able to extensively encompass many meanings within a few words.
The latter two lines manifest the supreme merit of being untainted and free from bondage.

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) refers to the clear recollection of all performed activities. As explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 57, commenting on a sūtra, it is defined as mindfulness, equal mindfulness, subsequent mindfulness, distinct mindfulness, and non-forgetting mindfulness.

The mind clearly retains [the object] without loss; this is the dharma of non-forgetfulness and non-loss. This meaning is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in the section on the Compendium of Synonyms (*Paryāya-saṃgraha*).

"Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the mind not being disturbed regarding its object. As the fifty-seventh [fascicle] states: "It causes the mind to be focused, to abide equally, to abide securely, and to abide closely."
This refers to "the nature of meditative concentration that is disciplined, tranquil, stilled, one-pointed, and even.
This is as explained in the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
As for "total retention," it is *dhāraṇī*.
Its essence consists of mindfulness and wisdom; because it can, with little effort, extensively encompass many meanings and maintain them all together, it is called *dhāraṇī*.
There are four kinds:
first, the dharma; second, the meaning; third, that which enables the attainment of bodhisattva-patience; and fourth, incantations (*mantra*).

Through mindfulness and clear recollection, one achieves non-forgetfulness; through meditative concentration, one is free from distraction and error, always abiding in a single state of focus; and through dhāraṇī, one encompasses all and can easily receive and expound the teachings. Thus, by means of a few dharmas, one can encompass vast dharmas.
The gateway of the knowledge of liberation refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); because it is free from the bonds of the tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called "liberation.
Liberation is itself non-obstruction; this non-obstructive liberation has wisdom as its essence.
Wisdom itself is the gate, for the gate of wisdom is able to enter the objects of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If expressed in terms of the gates of liberation, it is subsumed under supramundane right knowledge (*lokottara-samyagjñāna*)."

The *Xianyang lun* states: "To speak merely of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as to wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, whether in a state of meditative concentration or in a distracted state."

If one speaks of the samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, they pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); they are exclusively states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and not distracted (*vikṣipta*), and consist solely of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) rather than that derived from hearing or reflection (*śrutamayī* or *cintāmayī*).

If one speaks of the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, they are exclusively uncontaminated and not contaminated; they are exclusively states of meditative concentration and not distracted, and consist solely of wisdom derived from cultivation rather than that derived from hearing or reflection.
Now, that which is called "liberation" is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) takes the grasped object (*parikalpita*) as its objective condition, because that [grasped object] lacks intrinsic nature.
The gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) takes the dependent nature (*paratantra*) as its objective condition, because one does not form wishes or seek anything within the three realms.
The signless gate (*animitta-mukha*) takes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as its object, because it contemplates suchness (*tathatā*) as being signless.

Alternatively, all three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa-mukha*) can take all three natures as their objects; or, there are various differences in the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), as explained in the *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot) and the twelfth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The two phrases from the ancient scripture may be combined as: "The mind constantly dwells in unimpeded liberation.

Unimpeded (*anāvaraṇa*) means being without obstruction, and liberation (*vimokṣa*) refers to the gate of wisdom; thus, it can be said that one establishes the gate of wisdom for unobstructed liberation, and the mind constantly dwells therein.

At first glance, it appears that one constantly dwells in those unimpeded liberations; however, this is actually a fixed [formulaic] arrangement that omits the present mindfulness and the dhāraṇī—these two.
By merging these two current items into one ancient phrase, the meaning remains incomplete.
Sūtra: "He attains the eloquence of the *sarvatragāminī-dhāraṇī*.
Commentary: This explains the merit of maturing the six types of eloquence (*ṣaṭ-pratibhāna*).
First is uninterrupted eloquence, because it flows in an unceasing succession;
second is superior eloquence, because it cannot be overcome or suppressed;
third is mindful eloquence, because it recalls the matters of the Dharma being taught.
Fourth is the eloquence of wisdom (*prajñā-pratibhāna*), because it analyzes all phenomena (*dharma*).
Fifth is the eloquence of meditative concentration (*samādhi-pratibhāna*), because it skillfully explains all states of meditative absorption.
Sixth is the eloquence of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇī-pratibhāna*), because it explains various meanings and so forth within a single syllable and so forth.
Since it is neither among the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) nor among the seven forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), it is established separately as the sixth.
The single character "eloquence" (*bian*) at the end [of the list] extends through the preceding and intermediate items.
This sixth eloquence is subsumed under the categories of Dharma and Meaning within the four analytical knowledges.
The first five discernments all belong to the category of "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*).
This first one belongs to the fourth of the seven discernments, "the unceasing.
This second one belongs to the seventh of the seven, because it is the most supreme and wondrous of all worlds.
This fourth [power] and that fifth [power], being free from error or confusion, both involve mindfulness and concentration.
According to their respective functions, they take subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence.
The old sūtra states: "Mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, eloquence, and non-interruption."

Mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇī constitute three; "uninterrupted eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) should be taken as a single category. Thus, two [of the four], namely *prajñā* (superior wisdom) and uninterrupted eloquence, are missing.
The ancient translation explains that the aforementioned three types of eloquence are uninterrupted, rather than being the uninterrupted eloquence itself.
